title: The Moorland Treaty Trick
markdown:
The heather was already up to their knees when Silas steered them left, into a patch of gloom where the moonlight seemed to shrink away. Tess felt the satchel’s strap bite her shoulder: not papers tonight, a treaty, a fragile promise between her people and the Northern Clans, due at the Watchtower before the first hint of dawn. Fail, and the truce would shatter like ice under a winter boot. The air hung thick with unspoken urgency. Owls had already begun.

Oren walked beside her, crook in hand, eyes usually lost in constellations now sharp. At the village edge he had murmured, voice soft as dried leaves, “The North Star will guide us true, no matter what any man might say or promise. The stars themselves are the oldest paths.” Behind them the inns’ lamplight clung like shy fireflies, a cozy contrast to the vast shadowed expanse. Ahead, Whisperwind Moor undulated in heather and gorse under a moon like a silver coin, watching with an ancient knowing eye.

Silas’s smile was as smooth as a polished river stone. His voice flowed like warm honey. “The moor is a fickle friend, but I know its moods like my own hands. We’ll be at the Northern Watchtower before the owls finish their last hoot. A simple journey, under this fine moon.”

Wind whispered secrets through rustling heather. Damp earth. Unseen night-blooming flowers. A faint shimmer, like dust from a wing, hung just above the ground. The moor stretched wild and ancient, long shadows dancing and playing tricks. They walked for a long while in that hush. Tess counted her father’s lessons in the rhythm of her boots: stony ground, then peat, then the give that meant water was not far. Oren named stars under his breath as if they were sheep he refused to lose.

“The Great Bear is almost directly overhead, just as I predicted. From our village, if we follow its point, we should be heading almost due north-west.”

Silas chuckled, low. “The stars are pretty lights, young Oren, I’ll grant you that. But they don’t tell you where the bogs lie hidden, or where the shadows are deepest. Trust my feet. They know this land, every root and rise.” Another friendly nudge, further left, deeper gloom.

A prickle of unease bloomed in Tess’s chest. Her father, a seasoned courier, had taught her to read the land, not only lines on a map. Oren, usually lost in celestial wanderings, was certain.

“Are you quite sure, Silas?” Sharper than she intended. “The North Star seems to be pointing more that way.” Her arm a steady line against the sky. “That looks more west than north-west to me.”

His smile tightened, a knot pulled too hard. The twinkle dimmed. “The moor plays tricks with the light, child. Mists play games with your eyes. Your shepherd’s eye sees what it wishes. Now, onward. The night is passing.” His pace quickened. The smooth stones of his words pressed them forward.

The tricks of the light began to feel like misdirection. His path led away from the faint welcoming glow of the distant Watchtower, toward a darker stretch where the wind whistled a lonely tune and carried a sharp metallic scent, like forgotten rust. Oren stopped, brow furrowed, gaze on the horizon.

“Silas. The constellation of the Hunter is setting on the western edge. If we were truly heading north-west, we should be seeing the jagged outline of the Cragtooth Peaks by now. We are heading directly toward the Black Mire. That is not the correct way.”

Silas turned slowly. The kind facade cracked, rock under thin ice. His eyes were chips of obsidian, moonlight and nothing more. “Clever boy,” he sneered, honey gone. “But stars don’t carry treaties. And neither will you, if you don’t listen to those who know how to make a path.” He brandished a rough-hewn club, its end darkened as if by fire. “The Northern Clans pay handsomely for valuable deliveries. A treaty? A prize indeed, worth more than a shepherd’s crook or a courier’s satchel.”

Tess’s heart leaped into her throat, a frantic bird. Her father’s rigorous training kicked in: assess, adapt, act. She grabbed Oren’s arm, fingers digging in. “Run.”

The satchel, a heavy burden a moment before, was now purpose, not hindrance. Oren, lighter and more agile than Silas, dodged and weaved through uneven treacherous terrain with a shepherd’s innate grace. Silas, heavier and less nimble, lumbered after them, grunts of exertion echoing in the suddenly hostile night, frustrated rage given a body.

“This way!” Oren’s voice sharp with adrenaline, pointing toward a dense tangled thicket of thorns that seemed utterly impassable, a wall of prickles. Silas, blinded by rage and the heat of the chase, crashed blindly toward it, intent on cornering them. Tess and Oren, nimble and intimately familiar with the moor’s hidden dips and rises, veered sharply right, scrambling down a steep grassy slope Silas, focused solely on his prey, missed entirely. He plunged headlong into unforgiving thorns. Furious roars became yelps of pain as brambles tore at him.

They did not stop. Over jagged rocks, over hidden gurgling streams, lungs burning, legs aching, treaty safe. The thrill of escape mingled with the fear of the chase. The moon began its slow descent, casting long mournful shadows that seemed to stretch and writhe. At last a rocky outcrop, and below it a faint steady light: the Northern Watchtower, a beacon in the fading dark.

They stumbled forward, breathless, trembling, mud-caked. Guards at the gate startled at their wild appearance, then recognized the distinctive satchel and Tess’s courier markings. Questions could wait. The treaty was delivered. Peace, for now, held against the encroaching night.

First pale streaks of dawn painted the east, a hesitant blush of pink and gold. Tess and Oren sat by the Watchtower’s crackling fire, sipping hot bitter herb tea. In growing light the moor looked a little less enchanted and a little more itself: heather, gorse, the dark stitch of the mire they had not entered. For a while neither spoke. A lark tried the new air and thought better of it. The fire popped. Somewhere below, a guard changed watch with a scrape of boots.

Oren looked up at the fading stars, a faint knowing smile. “They showed us the way, Tess. Always.”

Tess nodded. A bittersweet ache settled in her chest. Silas’s smooth voice would stay, and so would the moon on Whisperwind, and so would the weight of a satchel that had been heavier than paper. She did not say the lesson out loud. She watched the last star go, and the tea steam, and the light on Oren’s crook, and let the new day arrive without a speech.
characters: Tess (a courier's daughter), Oren (a stargazing shepherd)
